clue.text: Index entry of multi-billionaire acquiring 25% of Mali's fruit

indicators.note: to acquire is to take something in, so one piece gets another placed inside it

parts.note: an index lists people surname first: Musk, Elon, the tech billionaire

indicators.note: a quarter of a four-letter word is its opening letter, so only one letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter: one of four letters is 25% of the word

explanation.surface: A rich man's shopping list: a billionaire buying up a quarter of an African country's fruit crop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Index entry' is the trick: an index lists a person surname first, then a comma and the forename, and the letter from the country slips in between the two names.
explanation.definitionFit: A muskmelon is a sweet orange-fleshed melon, such as the cantaloupe, a kind of fruit.

clue.text: View of distant terrain shows crack on promontory

parts.note: someone who bares their backside to onlookers moons them
a cape is a headland jutting into the sea

explanation.surface: A geologist's report: a fissure in a headland seen in some faraway landscape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' looks like a fissure in the rock, but it is the cleft between the buttocks, and showing it to people is a cheeky schoolboy prank with its own verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A moonscape is the lunar surface as seen, a landscape far away from Earth; hence a view of remote ground.

clue.text: In prison, heart's uplifted by a stringed instrument

indicators.note: only the central part is raised, and in a down clue lifting letters makes them read bottom to top
'by' here means beside, placing the extra letter alongside inside the word

parts.note: stir is slang for a jail
the article, taken as it stands

explanation.surface: A prisoner's spirits are lifted by music, played on a stringed instrument in the cell.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the middle two letters of the jail word are turned over, not the whole word; the article then slots in just before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The sitar is the long-necked Indian lute with many strings, plucked with a wire pick.

clue.text: Shrill cries from goal upset our wimpish striker initially

indicators.note: to upset is to knock over, and in a down clue that turns letters upside down

parts.note: an aim is a goal

indicators.note: 'initially' asks for the opening letter of each word in the run

parts.note: the opening letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Football: a feeble centre-forward misses, and the crowd lets out shrill cries of derision.
explanation.walkthrough: The football picture suggests jeers from the terraces; the cries are really a cat's. AIM turned up is MIA, then OWS.
explanation.definitionFit: Miaows are the high-pitched calls a cat makes, fairly described as piercing noises.

clue.text: Third book an unlikely success, opening being omitted

indicators.note: leaving out the opening drops the first letter of the word

parts.note: a fluke is a stroke of luck, success nobody expected

explanation.surface: A publisher's tale: an author's third novel becomes a surprise hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Third book' reads as a novelist's third title; it means the third book of the New Testament. FLUKE loses its F.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gospel of Luke follows Matthew and Mark as the third book of the New Testament.

clue.text: Fuzz call round family at dinner … one's an accessory

indicators.note: to go round something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: nap is the fuzzy raised pile on cloth
to ring someone is to call them on the phone
kin are relatives

explanation.surface: The police drop in on a family's dinner, making the fuzz an accessory to the meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fuzz' is British slang for the police, but here it is the soft pile on cloth. The first and third words of the clue together go round the relatives.
explanation.definitionFit: A napkin ring is a band holding a folded serviette, an ornamental item set out on the table.

clue.text: Dell Computers control data around office terminals

indicators.note: terminals are end points, so each word gives up its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of each of these five words

explanation.surface: A tech firm's machines run the data flowing around the office's workstations.
explanation.walkthrough: Dell looks like the computer maker attached to 'Computers', but it stands alone as the definition: a small wooded valley. 'Terminals' also looks like screens.
explanation.definitionFit: A slade is a dialect word for a little valley or hollow, the same thing as a dell.

clue.text: S Coe's rival, bolstered by medicine, went very quickly

indicators.note: in a down clue, being bolstered means having support placed underneath

parts.note: Steve Cram, British miler who raced Seb Coe in the 1980s
med is short for medical or medicine

explanation.surface: A doping story: a runner who raced Seb Coe, helped by drugs, sped round the track.
explanation.walkthrough: Seb Coe and Steve Cram were the great British middle-distance rivals of the 1980s; with his initial, S Cram. MED sits beneath.
explanation.definitionFit: To scram is to leave in a hurry, so scrammed is past tense for dashing off fast.

clue.text: Dad's taken aback by servant admitting close attachment

indicators.note: taken aback is read literally as carried backwards, so letters run the other way

parts.note: pa is a father

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a page is a boy attendant
the close of something is its end

explanation.surface: Father is startled when a servant confesses to a close attachment, perhaps a romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken aback' means surprised on the surface, but turns PA round; 'close attachment' reads as an affair, yet 'close' belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An appendage is a thing joined on to something larger, such as a limb or an add-on.

clue.text: Beermakers rejecting bronze vessels

indicators.note: to reject is to throw out, so some letters are removed

parts.note: brewers make beer
the opening two letters of the metal's name, a loose shortening by the setter

explanation.surface: Brewers turn down bronze containers for their ale, perhaps preferring steel or oak.
explanation.walkthrough: The bronze looks like the metal the vessels are made of; it only supplies the two letters that come off BREWERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Ewers are large jugs with wide spouts, traditionally for washing water: containers for liquid.

clue.text: Public fund for remote area

parts.note: a secret that is out is public
to back a venture is to finance it

explanation.surface: Government money earmarked for a far-flung region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Public fund' reads as a noun phrase about taxpayers' money; split it into two words meaning 'known' and 'finance'.
explanation.definitionFit: The outback is the sparsely populated interior of Australia, far from towns: remote country.

clue.text: Post Office board member, gutless, told sanctimonious untruth

indicators.note: a word without its guts has lost its middle letters

parts.note: the standard abbreviation
a rook is a piece on a chessboard

indicators.note: something told is spoken, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: pi is crossword shorthand for pious or sanctimonious

explanation.surface: A Post Office director, lacking courage, told a self-righteous lie; the Horizon scandal comes to mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board member' looks like a company director but is a chess piece, ROOK emptied to RK. PORK PIE is British rhyming slang: pork pie, lie (a porky).
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney rhyming slang a pork pie, or porky, stands for a lie, a falsehood.

clue.text: Small men? Ultimately hopeless mates

parts.note: s is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
a crew is a team of men working a ship

indicators.note: 'ultimately' means at the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Short men are useless partners, runs the cruel joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mates' looks like a noun for friends; it is a verb, having sex with, which the vulgar sense of the answer matches.
explanation.definitionFit: Screws is coarse slang for has sex with, which is what an animal does when it mates.

clue.text: Restless inmates start to lodge complaints

indicators.note: something restless will not keep still, so the letters move about

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Agitated prisoners begin filing grievances with the governor.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'complaints' formal grievances; the definition takes them as illnesses.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint in the medical sense is an illness or disorder, just as an ailment is.

clue.text: Voicing support, boss at paper protects nut like Coot?

indicators.note: a guard protects from behind, so one piece follows the other in line
voicing a word means saying it, so only its sound counts

parts.note: to bear a load is to support it
nut is slang for the head
the editor runs a newspaper

explanation.surface: An editor voices support for the setter, protecting the loony: a newspaper sticking up for its puzzler.
explanation.walkthrough: Coot is the setter, and a coot is a bird with a bald white forehead: 'bald as a coot' is a British simile. So the setter is joking about his own hairless head.
explanation.definitionFit: Bareheaded means with no hat on, head uncovered, which suits someone as bald as a coot.

clue.text: Artist repulsed by Coot's fatigued body?

indicators.note: something repulsed is driven back, so its letters run the other way

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician
Coot is the setter, so his is 'my'

explanation.surface: The setter complains that a painter is put off by his tired, worn-out physique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fatigued' reads as exhausted; the question mark flags the other sense, dressed in fatigues, the battle uniform. The body is a body of soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: An army is an organised force of troops, and soldiers wear fatigues as working uniform.

clue.text: Charades in areas of garden where top Republican's married

indicators.note: the top of a down entry is its first letter, which is the one swapped out

parts.note: rockeries are garden beds of stones and alpine plants
R is the usual abbreviation
m is the standard abbreviation for married

explanation.surface: Party games played out in the garden, where the leading Republican got wed.
explanation.walkthrough: ''s married' reads as 'is married': the R at the top of ROCKERIES becomes M. 'Charades' tempts toward the party game; here it means shams.
explanation.definitionFit: A charade can be an absurd pretence, a travesty or farce, which is what a mockery is.

clue.text: Worker who's not paid for licence

definitions.meaning: a hand is a worker, and one working for nothing is free
licence as liberty to act as you choose

explanation.surface: An unpaid volunteer looking for a permit.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is whimsical: taken literally, the phrase describes an unpaid labourer.
explanation.definitionFit: Having complete freedom to act as one sees fit is exactly what licence means in this sense.

clue.text: Confused and bothered having mounted debts

indicators.note: in a down clue, something mounted climbs upward, reading from the bottom

parts.note: riled means annoyed
IOUs are written acknowledgements of money owed

explanation.surface: Someone muddled and upset as their bills pile up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mounted debts' reads as debts piling up; 'mounted' in fact lifts the word before it, and 'having' lets IOUS follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Delirious means in a state of wild mental disturbance, bewildered and incoherent, as with a fever.

clue.text: They protect big races subject to disruption

indicators.note: disrupted things are thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Stewards guard major sporting events that might be disrupted by protesters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They protect' reads like police or stewards at an event; it is a bare, deliberately vague definition of bony cages.
explanation.definitionFit: Ribcages are the bony frames enclosing the heart and lungs, shielding those organs from harm.

clue.text: Description of space left audience flabbergasted

indicators.note: someone flabbergasted is thrown into confusion, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: L is the usual abbreviation
anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A talk on outer space leaves the listeners astonished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Description of space' suggests astronomy; it is geometry, and 'left audience' reads as a verb phrase when it gives L plus the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Euclidean geometry, from Euclid's axioms, is the classic flat mathematical model describing physical dimensions.

clue.text: Secure time away from nick

indicators.note: something away from a word has been taken out of it

parts.note: nick is British slang for steal
t is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A prisoner wins a spell outside the police station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a police station or prison (British slang for both); here it is the verb 'steal', which loses its T.
explanation.definitionFit: To seal something is to close it tightly and make it fast, one sense of making it safe.

clue.text: Conflict concerning new underground accommodation

parts.note: a war is armed conflict
re means about, as in letter headings
n is short for new

explanation.surface: A dispute about fresh bunker housing, perhaps a wartime shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests bomb shelters, which fits WAR; the accommodation is for rabbits.
explanation.definitionFit: A warren is the network of burrows where rabbits live, dug beneath the ground.

clue.text: Tradesman female singer permitted inside

indicators.note: a piece that goes inside another is enclosed by it

parts.note: f is the abbreviation for female
Cher, the American pop star
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper lets a woman vocalist come into his premises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Female singer' is one unit, the abbreviation followed by the pop star's name, and the word for permitted goes inside that unit, just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A fletcher is a maker of arrows, a craftsman of an old trade that survives as a surname.

clue.text: Maybe trawl centre of Croydon for suspect

parts.note: trawling is one way to fish, hence 'maybe'

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter

parts.note: the middle letter of the seven

explanation.surface: Police combing the heart of a south London town for a suspect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trawl' and 'suspect' paint a police hunt; the answer is an adjective. Croydon is a large town in south London.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fishy arouses doubt, seems dubious or questionable, as a suspect story would.

clue.text: He'll attract attention breakdancing, right?

indicators.note: letters that dance move about and change places

parts.note: the first five letters of the word are the fodder; its tail is the signal
r is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A street performer spinning on his head will draw a crowd, won't he?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breakdancing' must be split into BREAK and its indicator 'dancing'; that is the whole trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A barker is a fairground tout who shouts to draw people into a show, drumming up custom.

clue.text: Unwrapped anklets carelessly and bent down

indicators.note: unwrapping takes off the outer layer, so the outside letters go
things handled carelessly end up jumbled

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone unwraps some ankle bracelets clumsily and stoops to put them on.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests opening a present; 'unwrapped' strips A and S from the ends before the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Knelt is the past tense of kneel, lowering yourself onto your knees, as in stooping.

clue.text: Perhaps the Prince of Wales possesses a recipe for cordial

indicators.note: to possess is to hold, so one piece is held within another

parts.note: Wm is the old written short form of William, the current Prince of Wales
the article as it stands
R is the pharmacist's abbreviation for recipe, as on prescriptions

explanation.surface: A royal owns a recipe for a fruit drink, a cordial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cordial' looks like a drink, reinforced by 'recipe'; it is the adjective meaning friendly. 'Perhaps' signals William is one example of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: A cordial welcome is friendly and hearty, which is what a warm welcome is.

clue.text: Drank drop of Scotch, not 13!

indicators.note: a drop is a tiny amount, so only one letter of the word is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the word
not bare-headed: wearing a wig

explanation.surface: Someone downed a nip of whisky, and the exclamation mark insists he was not bald about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 is the answer at 13 down, meaning with head uncovered; its opposite here is having a wig on.
explanation.definitionFit: To swig is to gulp a drink in big mouthfuls, so swigged is a past tense of drinking.

clue.text: Accept welcome in Lagos, avoiding odd characters

indicators.note: 'in' places one piece inside another
skipping the odd-numbered letters keeps only the even ones

parts.note: the second and fourth letters
to greet someone is to welcome them

explanation.surface: Accepting a warm reception in Nigeria while steering clear of strange people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd characters' look like eccentrics; they are the odd-numbered letters of Lagos, which leave A and O around GREET.
explanation.definitionFit: To agree to a proposal is to consent or say yes to it, one sense of accepting it.

clue.text: Those favouring the end of poverty reassess periodically

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of the word

indicators.note: periodically means at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: Campaigners for ending poverty review their plans at regular intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The end of poverty' reads as an aim of policy; it is only its last letter. The definition treats votes in favour as people.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeses are affirmative votes or those who cast them, the supporters in a ballot.

clue.text: Overlooks appointments when penning love notes

indicators.note: to pen something is to shut it in, like an animal in an enclosure

parts.note: dates are engagements
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
minutes are the notes of a meeting, abbreviated min

explanation.surface: Someone forgets their engagements while writing romantic letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love notes' looks like billets-doux; 'notes' are minutes (MIN). 'Overlooks' is not 'misses' but 'towers over'.
explanation.definitionFit: A building that dominates a scene rises above it and commands the view, as a castle overlooks a town.
